blocks.md: This lesson follows **Historical Perspective and Further Reading** in *Sensor Perception* (Vol IV).

blocks.source: Vol IV, Sensor Perception, § Historical Perspective and Further Reading
blocks.md: The geometric foundations of computer vision trace back to photogrammetry and geodesy, where surveyors established rigorous mathematical formulations for optical distortion and perspective projection long before digital processors or mobile robots existed. In the late 1980s, @tsai1987versatile made accurate geometric calibration feasible on off-the-shelf industrial cameras and lenses by developing computationally efficient two-stage optimization algorithms. A decade later, @zhang2000flexible democratized the process by demonstrating that a camera could recover its intrinsic parameters and radial distortion from a planar checkerboard pattern observed at several unconstrained orientations.

questions.q: The section **Historical Perspective and Further Reading** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Detectable faults raise flags and age out honestly, while silent failures (saturation, contamination, fog backscatter, a misdated frame) deliver valid tensors, so the design must convert silent modes into detectable ones.

Learned depth and semantic confidence are not metric evidence, so a learned head may classify and propose but the range that enters a clearance check comes from qualified metric sensing, which can veto.
Out-of-distribution and input-support monitors flag into the health bitmask and can demote a camera to LiDAR-only operation, but they cannot certify what the transducer itself got wrong.
Every metric claim rests on intrinsics, extrinsics, and inter-sensor time offsets composed along a frame tree at the capture instant, and angular and timing errors scale with range and turn rate.
